formation.title: The Restoration of the Regnum
formation.text:
Granada has fallen. Narbonne answers to a court on the meseta. The lawyers have the Fuero Juzgo open on the table, and the chroniclers of Alfonso III at their elbow, and between them they will tell you that the kingdom of the Goths was never dissolved: only interrupted, for seven hundred and eighty years, by an occupation that no council ever ratified.

What remains is to say the name aloud, and the name is the whole argument.

In Latin it is Regnum Gothorum, the kingdom of the councils and the code. That is the state of Reccared and Recceswinth, whose law bound Goth and Roman alike because it was territorial and not personal, whose bishops legislated beside the palatine counts at Toledo, and whose see holds primacy over every church in the peninsula. It is a claim of continuous jurisdiction, and it is argued in the language the claim was written in.

In the tongue of Wulfila it is Reiki Gutane, the rule of the Goths. That is a different claim entirely: not an office inherited but a people surviving, with a name of its own, a king who holds the crown by the oath of his sworn men, and no need of Rome to say so. The Latin apparatus was always borrowed clothing. Take it off.

This choice unlocks a destiny path in the Traditions tab.

options.text: Regnum Gothorum: the kingdom of the councils and the code

modifiers.name: Regnum Gothorum
modifiers.text: The restored kingdom is a juridical person: the councils, the code, and the primacy of Toledo, continuous with Reccared. The crown that rules through the councils does not rule alone.

options.text: Reiki Gutane: the rule of the Goths, in the tongue of Wulfila

modifiers.name: Reiki Gutane
modifiers.text: The kingdom named in the tongue of Wulfila. A people rather than an office, a king held by the oath of his sworn men, and a name that Latin Christendom hears as an archaism.

advances.name: Liber Iudiciorum
advances.text: The code of Chindasuinth and Recceswinth, promulgated in 654 after revision at the Eighth Council of Toledo. Its innovation was territoriality: one law over Goth and Roman alike, replacing a system in which ancestry decided which book was opened over a man.

event.title: The Book of Judgements
event.text:
Chindasuinth began it in 642 and Recceswinth promulgated it in 654, after the bishops at the Eighth Council of Toledo had gone through it title by title. Twelve books, fifty-three titles, five hundred and twenty-six laws, all of it in Latin.

Its novelty was not what it said but whom it bound. Before it, a Goth was tried by Gothic custom and a Roman by the Breviary of Alaric, and a man's ancestry decided which book was opened over him. The Liber ended that. One code, one jurisdiction, every subject of the crown inside it, and a clause forbidding any judge to cite any other law at all.

That last clause is the one your jurists are arguing about.

options.text: Let no other law be cited in any court of the realm

modifiers.name: Let No Other Law Be Cited
modifiers.text: Recceswinth's clause enforced to the letter. Every court in the realm opens the same book, and the local customs the magnates lived by are simply not admissible.

options.text: The code takes in the customs it finds and outlives them

modifiers.name: The Code Takes In What It Finds
modifiers.text: The Liber is applied where it fits and glossed where it does not. Slower, but nobody is told their grandfather's law was never law.

advances.name: Councils of Toledo
advances.text: Eighteen synods between 400 and 702, convoked by the king and attended by bishops, abbots and the counts of the palatine office. Their canons were promulgated as royal law, making them the only body in post-Roman Europe that legislated for church and crown at once.

event.title: The Councils of Toledo
event.text:
Eighteen of them between 400 and 702, and they were never merely synods. The king convoked them. Bishops and abbots came, and so did the counts of the palatine office and the lay magnates of the realm, and what they agreed was published as the law of the kingdom.

At the third, in 589, Reccared read out his abjuration of Arianism and the kingdom changed religion in a room. At the fourth, in 633, Isidore of Seville presided and the seventy-fifth canon made the kingship formally elective and laid an anathema on any man who took the crown by violence. No other successor state to Rome built an institution that legislated for church and crown at once, and none of them lasted as long in one place.

The question your court cannot avoid is which half of that body actually holds the pen.

options.text: The council legislates and the king promulgates

modifiers.name: The Council Legislates
modifiers.text: The canons of Toledo are the law of the kingdom, and the men who write them wear mitres.

options.text: The king convokes and the council confirms

modifiers.name: The King Convokes
modifiers.text: The council is a royal instrument, as its first canon says. It meets when the crown has business for it.

advances.name: The Muster of the Whole People
advances.text: Wamba's military law of 673, revised by Ervig in 681. It binds general, count and gardingus, Goth and Roman, freeman and manumitted slave, and in Wamba's original text bishops and their retainers as well. No other early medieval kingdom conscripted across ethnicity, clergy and servile status at once.

advances.name: The Gardingi
advances.text: The sworn men of the royal household, holding their rank from a personal oath rather than from land tenure. Ervig's muster law names them as an order beside dukes and counts. They were the crown's counterweight to a nobility that elected kings and unmade them.

advances.name: The Clausurae
advances.text: The Gothic pass closures at Panissars and through the Corberes defiles: walls across defiles rather than castles on hills. Wamba forced them in 673 to recover Septimania, and they were the last barrier the Arab-Berber columns crossed in 719.

advances.name: The Royal Goldsmiths
advances.text: The workshops that produced the Guarrazar treasure: twenty-six votive crowns and crosses in gold, sapphire, pearl and cloisonne garnet, hung above altars rather than worn, and buried outside Toledo in 711.

advances.name: The Charity of Masona
advances.text: Masona of Merida, a Goth by birth, founded a hospital around 580 with salaried physicians, open to every comer, Christian and Jew alike, funded from a fixed share of the see's revenue and lending to the poor from a revolving fund.

advances.name: The Regal Coinage
advances.text: From about 575 Leovigild struck his own name on the tremissis and the mint city on the reverse, breaking with imitative imperial issues. Nearly a hundred mints served the kingdom, sited where tax was gathered and where armies moved.

advances.name: The Code as Charter
advances.text: Ferdinand III had the Liber translated into Castilian and granted it as the municipal fuero of Cordoba in 1241, then of Seville and Murcia. A conquered city was not given a new law; it was told which law it had always been under.

event.title: The Code as a City Charter
event.text:
When Ferdinand III took Cordoba in 1236 he did not give the city a new law. He had the Liber translated into Castilian and handed it over as the city's fuero, and did the same at Seville and Murcia and a string of towns after them.

The move is subtler than it looks. A conquered city given a new charter knows it has been conquered. A city handed the Fuero Juzgo is being told that it was always under this law, that the interruption was the anomaly, and that the crown has come back rather than come in. Incorporation by legal fiction costs nothing and works on people who would resist a garrison.

Whether to keep doing it is now a decision with a price, because a town that keeps its own charter pays for the privilege.

options.text: Grant the Fuero Juzgo to every town we take

modifiers.name: The Fuero Juzgo Granted
modifiers.text: Every town taken is handed the code as its charter, and told it was always under this law. Incorporation by legal fiction, at the price of a printing.

options.text: Confirm the towns in their own charters and take the fee

modifiers.name: The Towns Confirmed
modifiers.text: Each town keeps its own charter under royal confirmation, and pays for the privilege in coin and loyalty.

advances.name: The Officium Palatinum
advances.text: The counts of the household, the treasury, the patrimony and the cubicle, with the royal notaries: a salaried ministerial court in an age of household government, sitting at the councils beside the bishops.

advances.name: Littera Toletana
advances.text: The Visigothic minuscule, the Iberian book hand that outlived the kingdom by four centuries and was displaced only when the Cluniac reform imposed Carolingian script after 1080. Everything the peninsula remembered of itself was written in it.

advances.name: Primacy of the Spains
advances.text: The bull Cunctis Sanctorum of 1088 restored to Toledo the primatial standing it held under the Gothic kings and named Bernard of Sedirac first primate. Braga, Tarragona and Compostela disputed it for centuries.

event.title: The Primacy of the Spains
event.text:
Alfonso VI took Toledo in 1085 and within three years Urban II had issued the bull Cunctis Sanctorum, restoring to its bishop the primatial standing he had held under the Gothic kings and naming Bernard of Sedirac first primate of the Spains.

A primacy is not honorific. It is a claim to jurisdiction over other metropolitans, to summon them, to hear appeals from their courts, to have the cross carried before you in their cathedrals. Braga disputed it for four centuries. Tarragona disputed it. Compostela built its own case out of an apostle's bones.

The argument for Toledo has always been the same one: the councils met here, and the law was written here, and the kingdom is the same kingdom.

options.text: Press the primacy until every see in Iberia bends

modifiers.name: The Primacy Pressed
modifiers.text: Braga is summoned, Tarragona is overruled, and the cross of Toledo goes before the primate in every cathedral of the peninsula. Nobody outside Iberia thanks us for it.

options.text: A primacy of honour, and the peace of the Spanish church

modifiers.name: A Primacy of Honour
modifiers.text: Toledo keeps the title and drops the jurisdiction. The Spanish church is at peace with itself for the first time in four hundred years.

advances.name: The Hispanic Rite
advances.text: The liturgy of Isidore and Ildefonsus, suppressed in favour of the Roman use in 1080 and surviving in six parishes of Toledo. Cisneros printed its missal in 1500 and endowed a cathedral chapel to sing it daily.

event.title: The Rite of Isidore
event.text:
The Hispanic liturgy is older than the kingdom that adopted it. Isidore shaped it, Ildefonsus and Julian of Toledo added to it, and it was sung in every church of the peninsula for five hundred years. Then Gregory VII suppressed it in 1080 in favour of the Roman use, and it survived in six parishes of Toledo and nowhere else on earth.

Cisneros would not let it die. In 1500 he printed the Missale Mixtum, in 1502 the breviary, and he endowed a chapel in the cathedral with thirteen chaplains whose whole duty was to sing the old mass daily, forever.

A kingdom that keeps its own rite keeps a claim that predates the reforming papacy. A kingdom that gives it up gains a friend in Rome. Both are true at once.

options.text: Endow the old rite and sing it daily in the cathedral

modifiers.name: The Old Rite Endowed
modifiers.text: Thirteen chaplains sing the mass of Isidore daily in the cathedral, out of a printed missal, in a liturgy older than the reformed papacy that once suppressed it.

options.text: Conform to the Roman use, and keep the chapel as memory

modifiers.name: Conformed to the Roman Use
modifiers.text: The realm sings what Rome sings, and the Mozarabic chapel keeps the old books as a memory rather than a practice.

advances.name: The Spatharii
advances.text: The sword-bearers of the palace, the standing guard of a court where the succession was elective and the previous king had often died of it. Julian of Toledo places them at Wamba's side on the march into Septimania.

advances.name: The Gothic Road
advances.text: Toledo sits in the middle of the meseta and Narbonne on the Gulf of Lion, and the only thing joining them is the old Roman trunk road through Zaragoza and the Pyrenean gates. Manned way-stations are the difference between one realm and two.

advances.name: The Law of All Peoples
advances.text: Recceswinth's code forbids citing any other law in a Gothic court. The point is not exclusion but reach: a subject's ancestry no longer decides his jurisdiction, so the realm can hold peoples it has not assimilated.

advances.name: Opus Interrasile
advances.text: The pierced goldwork and hanging pendilia of the later Guarrazar crowns, a Byzantine technique the Toledan workshops took over and kept. Sapphire and pearl replace garnet, which is the kingdom's trade reach showing in its jewellery.

advances.name: The Council Made Permanent
advances.text: Eighteen councils across three centuries all met because a king wanted them to. A council that sits by right rather than by summons is a different institution, and the Gothic precedent is the one argument a crown cannot refuse without denying its own title.

event.title: The Council Made Permanent
event.text:
Eighteen councils in three hundred years means one every seventeen years, and always because a king wanted something from them. The bishops came when they were called and went home when they were dismissed, and in the gaps the crown legislated alone.

The magnates and the primate have now made the obvious argument. If the councils are the kingdom's constitution, and if the crown's own title rests on being the heir of the men who sat at them, then a council that sits only when summoned is not a constitution at all. It is a favour.

The crown may agree, and be bound. Or it may point out that the councils were royal from the first canon onward, and that a king who cannot dismiss an assembly is not the king the Goths elected.

options.text: The council sits by right and cannot be dismissed

modifiers.name: The Council Sits by Right
modifiers.text: An assembly the crown cannot dismiss, sitting on the precedent of Toledo. The kingdom now has a constitution and knows it.

options.text: The council sits when summoned, as it always did

modifiers.name: The Council Sits by Summons
modifiers.text: The councils were royal from the first canon onward. The crown intends to keep them that way.

advances.name: The General Host
advances.text: The muster clause of the code restated for an age of firearms. Every free subject still owes service, and the roll is kept by the same city courts that keep the land registers.

advances.name: The Septimanian March
advances.text: The Gothic province in Gaul: seven sees from Narbonne to Nimes, held for two centuries after Toulouse was lost at Vouille in 507. Holding it means garrisoning the far side of a mountain range against whoever rules the Rhone.

advances.name: The Narbonne Staple
advances.text: Septimania's value was never its farmland. Narbonne was the Roman trunk port of southern Gaul and the junction where the Via Domitia met the Via Aquitania, and a crown holding both ends of that road taxes the traffic without needing a fleet.

advances.name: National Jurisprudence
advances.text: Villadiego printed the Fuero Juzgo with commentary in 1600 and advocates argued from it in open court. A kingdom whose working law is a seventh-century code does not need to invent a legal tradition, only a faculty to teach the one it has.

advances.name: The Royal Unction
advances.text: Quiricus of Toledo anointed Wamba on 19 September 672, the first consecration of a king at his accession in the Latin West, eighty-two years before Pepin the Short. It made the king's person sacred without making his office hereditary.

event.title: The Anointing of Wamba
event.text:
Recceswinth died at Gerticos in September 672 and the magnates with him acclaimed Wamba on the spot, an old man who by every account did not want it. He refused until a duke drew a sword on him.

Then he did something no king in the Latin West had done. He went to Toledo, and on the nineteenth of September, in the church of the Praetorian Saints Peter and Paul, Quiricus the metropolitan poured oil on his head. Eighty-two years before Pepin the Short, in a kingdom the Franks called barbarous, a king was consecrated by the church at his accession.

It made his person sacred. It did not make his office hereditary. The Goths went on electing their kings, and going on killing them, and the two facts sat side by side for the rest of the kingdom's life.

options.text: Let the oil be poured, as it was at Toledo

modifiers.name: The Unction of Wamba
modifiers.text: Oil poured by the metropolitan of Toledo on 19 September 672, eighty-two years before any Frankish king was consecrated the same way. The person of the king is now sacred. The office is still elective.

advances.name: The Primatial Chancery
advances.text: A see claiming jurisdiction over every other metropolitan in the peninsula needs an apparatus to exercise it. By the eighteenth century Toledo's was the largest ecclesiastical administration in Iberia.

advances.name: The Royal Retinue
advances.text: The gardingi did not disappear. They were re-established as the household horse of an absolutist court, drawn from the same families, holding a commission where their ancestors held an oath.

advances.name: The Academy Edition
advances.text: The Real Academia Espanola printed the Fuero Juzgo in 1815 with the Latin and the Castilian on facing pages, and antiquarians argued over whether the kingdom's oldest law was also its most liberal.

advances.name: The Civil Code
advances.text: The Liber's territorial principle carried to its conclusion: every inhabitant of the realm tried by one law regardless of descent. In the seventh century that meant Goth and Roman; in the nineteenth it means everyone else.

event.title: One Law for Every Inhabitant
event.text:
The Real Academia printed the Fuero Juzgo in 1815 with the Latin and the Castilian on facing pages, and the men writing constitutions found something inconvenient in it. The oldest law in Europe already said what they were arguing for: that the law is territorial, that it binds every inhabitant of the realm, and that a man's descent does not decide which court he stands in.

In 654 that meant Goth and Roman. It is not obvious what it means now, and that is exactly the fight.

One reading makes the code a living instrument and applies its principle to everyone the realm has since acquired. The other makes it a monument: the nation's oldest possession, studied and honoured, and left where it is.

options.text: The principle is living law and binds everyone we hold

modifiers.name: The Principle Is Living Law
modifiers.text: Territorial jurisdiction carried to its conclusion. In 654 it meant Goth and Roman; now it means everyone the realm holds.

options.text: The code is the nation's oldest inheritance, and a monument

modifiers.name: The Oldest Inheritance
modifiers.text: The Fuero Juzgo studied, printed and honoured as the nation's founding document, and left exactly where it stands.

advances.name: National Conscription
advances.text: The muster clause outlives every other article of the code, because every state eventually wants it. The kingdom that has conscripted its whole free population since 673 simply keeps the rolls.

advances.name: The Gothic Revival
advances.text: The nineteenth century dug up Guarrazar and sent the crowns to Paris and Madrid, and the Toledan workshops answered with a trade in damascened and cloisonne reproduction. Antiquarianism became an export.

destiny.name: The Sickness of the Goths
destiny.text:
Canon 75 of the Fourth Council of Toledo, in 633, laid down that a king is raised by the common consent of the magnates and the bishops of the whole people, and pronounced anathema on any man who took the crown otherwise. In the seventy years that followed, kings were deposed, blinded, tonsured and murdered until the Franks had a name for the habit: the sickness of the Goths.

Everything else in the restored constitution is settled. The code is written, the councils have their canons, the primate has his see. Only the making of a king is open, and until the realm closes it every accession is a war waiting for a candidate.

Requires: a stable realm.

event.title: The Sickness of the Goths
event.text:
Your jurists have the canons open again, and this time there is nothing to argue about. The seventy-fifth canon of Toledo IV is unambiguous. The king is raised by the common consent of the magnates and the bishops of the whole people. He is not born to it.

Then they turn the page and read the rest of the century. Chindasuinth took the throne from Tulga in a coup and had two hundred noble families destroyed to keep it. Wamba was tonsured while unconscious and woke up a monk. Ervig produced a deathbed abdication nobody believed. Witiza's sons were still fighting Roderic when the ships came over from Africa, and the Franks wrote the whole thing down under one heading: morbus Gothorum, the sickness of the Goths, the disease of killing your kings.

The restored kingdom has inherited the title, the code, the councils and the primacy. It has also inherited this. Nothing in the constitution says how a Gothic king is made, and until something does, every deathbed in Toledo is a mobilisation.

options.text: Then let the realm settle it, and settle it for good

destiny.name: The Seventy-Fifth Canon
destiny.text:
Isidore of Seville presided at Toledo in 633 and the seventy-fifth canon is his work: the king is raised by the common consent of the magnates and the bishops of the whole people, and whoever seizes the throne by any other means is cast out of the church and out of the kingdom.

Read the wording closely. It says the bishops of the whole people, and the whole people includes the Gothic sees beyond the mountains. An election held while a third of the episcopate answers to a foreign crown is not the election the canon describes. Narbonne is already yours. Its suffragans are not.

Requires: Béziers and Agde, and a stable realm.

conditions.text: Own Béziers, or a subject owns it
Own Agde, or a subject owns it

event.title: Anathema
event.text:
The canon is read out in full at the opening of the council, in the form Isidore left it. The king shall be raised by the common consent of the magnates and the bishops of the whole people. Whoever seizes the crown by tyranny, by usurpation, by oath sworn to a faction or by the blood of a predecessor is anathema before God and cast out from the church and from the whole assembly of Christians with all the accomplices of his impiety.

The bishops rise and repeat it, and the magnates rise and repeat it, and for the first time since 711 the sentence has an assembly behind it that can actually pronounce it. What they have made is not a ceremony. It is an electorate, and every man in the room now knows that a claimant without their votes is not a rival king but an excommunicate with an army.

The Septimanian bishops sit with them. They were the point. The canon says the whole people, and a Gothic election held without the sees beyond the mountains would have been exactly the sort of faction the canon condemns.

options.text: Let no man be king who is not made king in this room

destiny.name: The Fisc and the Patrimony
destiny.text:
At the Eighth Council of Toledo in 653 the bishops were handed the most awkward question a court can be asked. Chindasuinth had confiscated on a scale that made his family rich, and his son Recceswinth laid the whole of it before the council rather than keep it quietly.

What came out was a rule that has no equal in any other successor kingdom. Whatever a king acquires after his accession belongs to the treasury of the realm and not to his heirs. His own inherited patrimony remains his own and passes as any man's does. A king who cannot leave the kingdom's revenue to his children has an office to hand on, and not an estate.

Requires: Lodève and Nîmes, a treasury of 2000, Toledo our capital again with a chancery in it, and a stable realm.

conditions.text: Own Lodève, or a subject owns it
Own Nîmes, or a subject owns it
Toledo is our capital and has a chancery

event.title: The Treasury and the Purse
event.text:
The estates of the late king are being counted, and the count has produced the question the councils answered in 653 and every court since has tried to forget.

Chindasuinth confiscated on a scale that left his family among the richest in the peninsula, and it was his own son Recceswinth who laid the ledgers before the Eighth Council of Toledo rather than inherit them quietly. The bishops separated the two heaps. What a king acquires after his accession he acquires as king, and it belongs to the treasury of the realm. What he inherited before it he holds as a man, and it passes to his children like anyone else's land.

That is the whole doctrine of the crown as an office, written in money instead of Latin. Your treasurers want to know which heap the current pile belongs in, and they would like it in writing.

options.text: What the crown takes belongs to the kingdom, not the king's heirs

modifiers.name: Fiscus Regni
modifiers.text: The treasury of the kingdom, audited by the council and closed to the royal household. Revenue rises because everyone can see where it goes, and the army waits its turn like everybody else.

options.text: The king keeps his own lands, and the realm is paid from them

modifiers.name: Patrimonium Regis
modifiers.text: The king keeps his inheritance and the realm is paid out of it. A royal domain worked hard, drained, planted and rebuilt, because every acre of it is the crown's own living.

destiny.name: The King Under the Code
destiny.text:
Isidore wrote it as wordplay and the lawyers took it as a rule of forfeiture. Rex eris si recte facias, si non facias non eris. You will be a king if you act rightly; if you do not, you will not be one.

A crown conferred by an assembly, out of a written code, is held on the code's terms and can be lost on them. This is the end of the argument the councils began: the office outlives the man, the law outranks the office, and the kingdom is a person in law that continues whoever wears the crown. It is not won with an army. It is won by being rich, lettered, stable and old.

Requires: an average literacy of 30, 3000 in the treasury, Toledo held and grown to 52 development, 75 prestige, and a stable realm.

conditions.text: Toledo is ours and its development is at least 52

event.title: Rex Eris Si Recte Facias
event.text:
The formula is Isidore's and it was never meant to be litigated. Rex eris si recte facias, si non facias non eris. You will be a king if you act rightly; if you do not, you will not be one. He was playing on the old etymology that derives rex from recte, and the lawyers have spent four centuries refusing to treat it as a joke.

Their argument is finished and it is airtight. The crown is conferred by an assembly. It is conferred out of a written code. What is granted on terms can be withdrawn on the same terms, and therefore the kingship is an office with conditions attached and not a possession at all.

The crown may accept that, swear to the code before the oil touches its head, and become the first monarchy in Europe that is formally answerable to its own law. Or it may accept the argument and reverse its direction: the code binds the realm, the crown is the code's judge and not its subject, and the officers who enforce it answer to the king.

options.text: The king swears to the code before the crown touches him

modifiers.name: Rex Eris
modifiers.text: A crown that swore to the code before it was crowned. Every chancery in Christendom now knows that treaties made with this kingdom outlive the man who signed them, and negotiates accordingly.

options.text: The code binds the realm, and the crown is the code's judge

modifiers.name: Lex Ministrorum
modifiers.text: The code enforced downward. The king's judges ride circuit, the king's men watch the judges, and the schools that produce them are the best endowed in the peninsula. The merchants pay for all of it.

destiny.name: The King Crowned in His Father's Life
destiny.text:
There is exactly one way a Gothic king ever beat the election, and it is not an argument. It is timing. Chindasuinth was eighty and Braulio of Zaragoza wrote urging him to it, and on the twentieth of January 649 his son Recceswinth was crowned beside him while he still breathed. Leovigild had done it for Hermenegild and Reccared; Egica did it for Wittiza. The sworn men swear to the son in the father's lifetime, and when the father dies there is nothing left to elect.

A king made by his own men owes them a war. The oldest debt in the kingdom is the strait, which Count Julian of Ceuta opened in 711 with his own ships.

Requires: Ceuta and Tangier, and an army of 30,000 men.

conditions.text: Own Ceuta, or a subject owns it
Own Tangier, or a subject owns it

event.title: The Son Crowned Beside the Father
event.text:
Braulio of Zaragoza wrote the letter that mattered. Chindasuinth was eighty, the realm was quiet for once, and the bishop put it to him plainly: name the boy now, while you can still make them swear.

On the twentieth of January 649 Recceswinth was crowned beside his living father, and four years later he inherited a kingdom without a single claimant riding for Toledo. It was not new. Leovigild had raised Hermenegild and Reccared in his own lifetime. Egica did the same for Wittiza. Association does not win the argument about elective kingship; it makes the argument irrelevant, because the men who would do the electing have already sworn.

So the oath is taken and the crown is on a boy's head, and the men who swore it want to be used. Across the water is Septem, which the Goths held until Count Julian sent his ships to fetch Tariq over in 711. There is no older debt in the kingdom.

options.text: The oath is sworn to the son. Now take them across the water

destiny.name: One People, Two Kingdoms
destiny.text:
The Goths parted at the Danube and were never formally two nations. Theodoric the Amal ruled Italy from Ravenna, married his daughter to the Visigothic king, and when that king fell at Vouillé in 507 took the Spanish kingdom into his own hand and held both until he died in 526. One Gothic realm from Sicily to the Tagus, for nineteen years.

A crown that claims a people rather than an office is claiming the people entire. The other half of it lies at Ravenna under a roof cut from a single stone, and Verona, which the German poets went on calling Bern for eight hundred years, was Theodoric's own city.

Requires: Ravenna and Verona, an army of 50,000 men, and 50 prestige.

conditions.text: Own Ravenna, or a subject owns it
Own Verona, or a subject owns it

event.title: The Amal Inheritance
event.text:
Ravenna is yours, and in the mausoleum outside the wall there is a roof cut from a single block of Istrian stone, three hundred tons of it, over an empty porphyry tub. The Arians were expelled and the body was thrown out long ago, but the Goths of the city know whose it was.

Theodoric the Amal ruled Italy for thirty three years, married his daughter to the Visigothic king, and after Vouillé took Spain into his own hand and held both realms until 526. It is the only time the gens was one polity, and the memory of it ran so deep that German poets were still singing about Dietrich von Bern, Theodoric of Verona, eight hundred years later.

A crown that claims a people rather than an office has just made good on that claim. What it does with the Italians is the question. Theodoric's own answer was civilitas: the Goths keep the sword, the Romans keep the pen, and neither takes up the other's work. The alternative is the one his people took when they first came in, and it is simpler. Give the sworn men their thirds of the land.

options.text: Settle the sworn men on the land, as the Amals did

modifiers.name: Sortes Gothicae
modifiers.text: The sworn men given their allotments, as the Goths took their thirds of Italy in 493. A landed warband musters faster and larger, and takes its wealth out of the soil instead of the road.

options.text: The Goths keep the sword and Italy keeps its offices

modifiers.name: Civilitas
modifiers.text: Theodoric's formula, kept as he kept it. The Goths hold the sword and the Romans hold the pen, and a war fought by one caste of the realm wears down the rest of it far less.

destiny.name: The Tongue Still Spoken
destiny.text:
In 1562 Ogier Ghiselin de Busbecq, the emperor's ambassador at Constantinople, fell into conversation with two envoys from the Crimea and wrote down eighty six of their words. Broe for bread. Ada for egg. Reghen for rain. Handa for hand.

He had found the last people on earth who spoke Gothic: a thousand years and three thousand miles from Toledo, in the mountains above the Black Sea, in a principality the Greeks called Theodoro and the maps still label Gothia. Kaffa below them is the Genoese port that is the gate to it.

An office would never recognise the obligation. A people does. Go and get them.

Requires: Theodoro and Kaffa, an army of 75,000 men, and 75 prestige.

conditions.text: Own Theodoro, or a subject owns it
Own Kaffa, or a subject owns it

event.title: Broe, Ada, Reghen, Handa
event.text:
The word list is a copy of a copy, and every clerk who reads it goes quiet.

In 1562 the emperor's ambassador at Constantinople, a Fleming named Busbecq who collected manuscripts and tulip bulbs, got into conversation with two envoys down from the Crimea. One was a Greek who had learned their speech; the other was one of them and had half forgotten it. Busbecq wrote down eighty six words. Broe, bread. Ada, egg. Reghen, rain. Handa, hand. Fyder, four. Ies, he is.

He knew exactly what he was holding. So do you. It is your language, spoken by farmers and vine dressers in the hills above the Black Sea, a thousand years and three thousand miles from the room where Reccared abjured Arianism, in a principality the Greeks called Theodoro and every map since has labelled Gothia.

The Ottomans starved Mangup out over five months in 1475. Your soldiers are standing in it now, and the people in the valley below still say ada when they mean an egg.

options.text: Bring them home, and let the people be one people again

modifiers.name: The Gathered Goths
modifiers.text: The Crimean Goths brought west and settled among their own. The ranks fill from a people rather than a province, and a crown that went three thousand miles for eighty six words is not a crown anyone forgets.

options.text: Leave them where they are and hold Gothia as a far march

modifiers.name: Marca Gothica
modifiers.text: Gothia held where it stands, garrisoned above the Black Sea and supplied by sea. The forts pay for themselves in claims; the factors who might have been trading elsewhere do not.

units.name: Thiufa
units.text: The levy of a thousand under its thiufadus, raised by legal compulsion across every rank of the free population. It holds its ground because breaking it costs a man his standing in law, and it fights like what it is: farmers, labourers and clerics with spears.
units.unlocked_by: The Muster of the Whole People

units.name: Gardingi
units.text: The king's sworn men, holding their rank from a personal oath rather than from land. They charge frontally, they break morale where they land, and they pay for both in casualties.

units.name: Spatharii
units.text: The sword-bearers of the palace, the standing guard of an elective monarchy that had buried too many kings. Immovable in a line and slow to move anywhere else.

units.name: Hueste del Fuero
units.text: The general host of the code with matchlocks. Called out from the same rolls the city courts keep for land, faster to raise than any contract army and made of townsmen rather than veterans.

units.name: Gardingos Reales
units.text: The household horse of an absolutist court, still sworn to the king's person and still drawn from the families that swore seven centuries ago. Splendid in the charge and poorly suited to a long campaign away from the court that pays them.

units.name: Milicia del Fuero
units.text: Universal conscription under the oldest conscription law in Europe. The rolls were already there when the rifles arrived.

buildings.name: Court of the Liber Iudiciorum
buildings.text: The court of the comes civitatis and his iudex, holding the certified copy of the code that Recceswinth's law required of every jurisdiction, and forbidden to open any other book.

buildings.name: Aula Regia
buildings.text: The palatine court and the hall of the councils: bishops, abbots, the counts of the household and the magnates of the realm, legislating together and publishing their canons as royal law. It stood at Toledo and could stand nowhere else.

effect_groups.label: To the country, when built in the capital

buildings.name: The Clausurae
buildings.text: Walls thrown across a mountain defile rather than a castle on a hill. The Gothic pass closures held the two halves of the kingdom together, and their fall in 719 ended it.

buildings.name: Royal Goldsmiths' Workshop
buildings.text: The workshops that hung crowns above altars: gold, sapphire, pearl and cloisonne garnet, with the king's name spelled out in letters dangling from the rim.

children.text: Gold is produced in the location's market
Gems is produced in the location's market
Silver is produced in the location's market

buildings.name: Xenodochium
buildings.text: An episcopal hospital on Masona's model, with salaried physicians, open to Christian and Jew alike, and lending to the poor from a fund the see replenishes every year.

buildings.name: Moneta Regia
buildings.text: A provincial mint striking the tremissis with the king's name on one face and the city's on the other. Its purpose is not bullion but jurisdiction: the crown made visible in a town it rarely visits.

buildings.name: Primatial See
buildings.text: The see that summons other metropolitans, hears appeals from their courts and has its cross carried before it in their cathedrals. There can be only one, and it argues its case from the councils.

effect_groups.label: To the country, when built in the capital

buildings.name: Mozarabic Chapel
buildings.text: A chapel endowed to sing the Hispanic rite daily out of a printed missal, keeping alive a liturgy that Rome suppressed and that six parishes of Toledo refused to give up.

buildings.name: Mansio Regia
buildings.text: A royal way-station on the Gothic road, a day's ride from the next one, where couriers change horses and the writ of a capital in the middle of the meseta keeps moving toward the sea.

buildings.name: Catedra del Fuero Juzgo
buildings.text: A faculty whose entire curriculum is one seventh-century book, and whose graduates fill the courts that apply it.

buildings.name: Thesaurus Publicus
buildings.text: The treasury of the kingdom, kept apart from the chamber of the king. What a king acquires after his accession is counted here and cannot be left to his children, which is the doctrine of the crown as an office stated in ledgers rather than in Latin.

buildings.name: Thiudangardi
buildings.text: Wulfila's Gothic word for kingdom, and it means the king's enclosure: a household and not an office. The hall where the sworn men are fed and quartered, and where an heir is acclaimed in his father's lifetime while the men who would otherwise elect him are standing in the room.

list.name: Numerarii of the Fisc
list.text: The tax establishment of the kingdom. The comes patrimonii at court appointed the numerarius of each city himself, for a term of one year, bypassing the province entirely: the fisc was the most centralised thing the Goths ran. The two Barcelona documents of 592, the De fisco Barcinonensi, record the bishops of Tarraconensis fixing what the collectors might take and what they might charge for taking it, and the Third Council of Toledo (589) had already ordered a provincial synod every year at which the fiscal agents answered for their conduct. The men who assessed the land were audited by the men who baptised it.

list.name: Episcopal Schools
list.text: Canon 1 of the Second Council of Toledo (527) ordered that boys given to the church be raised in a house attached to the cathedral, under the bishop's eye and a teacher's, until they were old enough to choose their own life. It is the earliest cathedral school on record anywhere in the Latin West. The Fourth Council (633) made the rule general, and what came out of those houses was Isidore's Etymologiae, the treatises of Ildefonsus and Julian, and the notarial hands that drafted the code.

list.name: Sacramentum Fidelitatis
list.text: The general oath of fidelity sworn to the king by the palatine office, the bishops and the people at every accession, set down in the written form the lawyers called conditiones sacramentorum. Recceswinth's code voided any oath sworn to a lord other than the king, a claim no monarchy north of the Pyrenees could make, since there the whole political order was built from exactly the private oaths this law annulled. Canon 75 of Toledo IV (633) put the anathema of the church behind it, and Egica laid his own oath before the Fifteenth Council in 688 to ask which part of it still bound him. The oath does not say who becomes king. It says the men who swore may not unmake one.

list.name: Conventus Publicus Vicinorum
list.text: The public assembly of the neighbours, the one jurisdiction the Liber Iudiciorum recognises below the count's court. A runaway had to be produced before it, a boundary proved before it, straying stock declared to it, and the lesser wrongs of a village settled in it by men who owed no lord for the right to judge. Its descendants are the village concilia of tenth century northern Iberia, which is why the rural clauses of a seventh century code were still working law four hundred years after the kingdom fell.
